cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 6 · Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse (IQN)

bullets.label: Maternal and Newborn Nursing — Student Learning Notes

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Level 2
cards.body: International maternity settings expect nurses to combine evidence-based assessment with cultural safety, structured escalation, multidisciplinary teamwork and informed family participation.

bullets.label: This level bridges national nursing preparation
bullets.text: This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations — strengthening your ability to interpret fetal and maternal trends, manage high-risk pregnancy, respond to obstetric emergencies and communicate clearly across teams.

bullets.label: Apply international standards for maternal and newborn assessment
Interpret fetal wellbeing and labour-progress information
Recognise and escalate high-risk pregnancy complications
Respond to obstetric emergencies and postpartum deterioration
Assess high-risk newborns and provide culturally safe, family-centred care

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: Safe. Culturally Responsive. Evidence-Informed.

bullets.label: By completing Level 2, you will be equipped to
bullets.text: By completing Level 2, you will be equipped to deliver maternity and newborn care that meets the professional expectations of international healthcare environments — integrating the woman's history, observations, fetal wellbeing, labour progress, newborn adaptation and family preferences.

bullets.label: Integrate evidence-based practice into every assessment
Meet global expectations for maternity nursing
Remain vigilant for rapid deterioration at all times

cards.title: SECTION 1
cards.body: High-Risk Pregnancy & Maternal Assessment

bullets.label: International maternity practice places strong
bullets.text: International maternity practice places strong emphasis on early risk identification, evidence-based monitoring and shared decision-making. High-risk pregnancy may involve hypertension, diabetes, placental problems, infection, fetal growth concerns or preterm labour.

cards.title: Section 1 Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Assess women with high-risk pregnancy conditions
Interpret maternal and fetal trends accurately
Recognise preeclampsia, diabetes and placental complications

cards.title: Core Concepts: High-Risk Pregnancy
cards.body: Hypertensive Disorders

bullets.label: Preeclampsia: hypertension, proteinuria,
bullets.text: Preeclampsia: hypertension, proteinuria, headache, visual disturbance, upper abdominal pain. Severe disease can progress to seizures, stroke or organ dysfunction.

bullets.label: Includes glucose monitoring, insulin or
bullets.text: Includes glucose monitoring, insulin or medication support, nutrition education and surveillance for maternal and fetal complications.

bullets.label: Placenta previa: painless bleeding. Abruption:
bullets.text: Placenta previa: painless bleeding. Abruption: pain, tenderness and bleeding. Avoid vaginal examination until placental location is confirmed.

bullets.label: Regular contractions, cervical change, leaking
bullets.text: Regular contractions, cervical change, leaking fluid or fetal growth and movement concerns before term require prompt evaluation.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: Severe Preeclampsia
cards.body: A woman at 35 weeks reports severe upper abdominal pain and visual disturbance. Her blood pressure is markedly elevated.

bullets.label: Nursing Response: Recognise severe preeclampsia
bullets.text: Nursing Response: Recognise severe preeclampsia → initiate urgent escalation → prepare prescribed treatment → monitor maternal and fetal status closely.

bullets.label: Severe hypertension symptoms require immediate action
No vaginal examination if placenta previa is possible
Use structured escalation and accurate records

cards.title: SECTION 2
cards.body: Responding to Obstetric Emergencies

bullets.label: Obstetric emergencies can develop suddenly and
bullets.text: Obstetric emergencies can develop suddenly and threaten the life of the mother, fetus or both. Effective nursing response requires rapid assessment, role clarity, teamwork and preparation for emergency birth or resuscitation.

cards.title: Obstetric Emergency: Core Concepts
cards.body: Postpartum Haemorrhage

bullets.label: Activate emergency response. Assess uterus, administer medications, prepare blood products and monitor continuously.
Relieve pressure on cord, reposition the woman, call for emergency assistance and prepare for urgent birth.
Immediate team response. Follow established manoeuvres or surgical pathways without delay.
Sudden hypoxia or collapse: initiate resuscitation, coordinate obstetric and critical-care support rapidly.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: Cord Prolapse
cards.body: After rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate falls sharply and the nurse sees the umbilical cord at the vaginal opening.

bullets.label: Relieve pressure on the cord per protocol
Reposition the woman to reduce compression
Activate help early. Communicate clearly during rapidly changing events.

cards.title: SECTION 3
cards.body: Caring for High-Risk Newborns

bullets.label: High-risk newborns may be premature, growth
bullets.text: High-risk newborns may be premature, growth restricted, hypoglycaemic, jaundiced, infected or experiencing respiratory distress. Their condition can deteriorate quickly — making close assessment and timely intervention essential.

cards.title: High-Risk Newborn: Core Concepts
cards.body: Prematurity & Low Birth Weight

bullets.label: Vulnerable to heat loss, respiratory
bullets.text: Vulnerable to heat loss, respiratory difficulty, infection, feeding problems and unstable blood glucose. Developmentally supportive care is essential.

bullets.label: Grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, central cyanosis or apnoea require immediate assessment and neonatal support.
Monitor at-risk newborns. Treat with feeding support, glucose therapy or phototherapy per severity and policy.
Temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy
bullets.text: Temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy or abnormal colour may indicate infection. Early escalation and treatment are critical.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: Premature Newborn in Distress
cards.body: A premature newborn develops grunting, chest retractions and falling oxygen saturation.

bullets.label: Subtle changes in a newborn can signal
bullets.text: Subtle changes in a newborn can signal significant deterioration. Maintain warmth, stabilise glucose and never delay escalation of respiratory distress. Include parents in care whenever clinically possible.

cards.title: SECTION 4
cards.body: Culturally Safe, Family-Centred Maternity Care

bullets.label: Maternity care occurs within personal, cultural
bullets.text: Maternity care occurs within personal, cultural and family contexts. International nurses must communicate respectfully, support informed choice and avoid assumptions about pregnancy, birth, feeding or family roles.

cards.title: Principles of Culturally Safe Care
cards.body: Cultural Safety

bullets.label: Ask what matters to the woman and family rather
bullets.text: Ask what matters to the woman and family rather than assuming preferences based on background. Accommodate cultural practices when clinically safe.

bullets.label: Provide clear information on options, benefits,
bullets.text: Provide clear information on options, benefits, risks and alternatives. Allow time for questions. Consent is an ongoing process — not a single event.

bullets.label: Use professional interpreters for complex or
bullets.text: Use professional interpreters for complex or high-risk discussions. Adapt information for literacy, hearing, vision or cognitive needs.

bullets.label: Pregnancy loss and neonatal illness can be
bullets.text: Pregnancy loss and neonatal illness can be traumatic. Provide compassionate communication, privacy and referral to appropriate support services.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: Urgent Caesarean with Language Barrier
cards.body: A woman with limited English requires an urgent caesarean birth.

bullets.label: The nurse arranges a professional interpreter,
bullets.text: The nurse arranges a professional interpreter, explains each step clearly, checks understanding and keeps the chosen support person involved wherever possible.

bullets.label: Urgency does not remove the need for respectful, informed and compassionate communication.
Respect individual preferences at every step
Always for complex or high-stakes conversations
Support participation even during urgent care

cards.title: Programme 6 Complete — Well Done!
cards.body: By completing GNPS Programme 6 Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to:

bullets.label: Assess, monitor and escalate maternal and fetal concerns
Respond rapidly with role clarity and team coordination
Stabilise and support high-risk neonates with confidence
Deliver respectful, family-centred, informed care globally
You are now ready for Level 3 — focusing on leadership, quality improvement and global maternal-newborn health.

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 6 · Maternal and Newborn Nursing

cards.title: Section 1
cards.body: High-Risk Pregnancy and Maternal Assessment

bullets.label: International maternity practice places strong
bullets.text: International maternity practice places strong emphasis on early risk identification, evidence-based monitoring, and shared decision-making. High-risk pregnancy may involve hypertension, diabetes, placental problems, infection, fetal growth concerns, or preterm labour.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you should be able to:

bullets.label: Evaluate women presenting with complex or high-risk pregnancy conditions
Analyse maternal and fetal monitoring data to identify deterioration
Identify preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, and placental problems
Apply structured communication tools and clear documentation

cards.title: Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy
cards.body: Recognising Preeclampsia

bullets.label: Preeclampsia may present with any combination of the following warning signs:
Abnormal laboratory results (platelets, liver enzymes, creatinine)
Severe disease can escalate rapidly to:
Treat severe hypertension symptoms as a clinical emergency. Escalate immediately.

cards.title: Gestational Diabetes
cards.body: Careful management of blood glucose protects both mother and baby. Nursing care includes:

bullets.label: Regular fasting and post-meal checks to guide treatment decisions
Oral agents or insulin therapy as prescribed; patient education on administration
Meal planning, carbohydrate awareness, and dietary guidance
Monitor for macrosomia, polyhydramnios, and neonatal hypoglycaemia

cards.title: Placental Complications
cards.body: Placenta Praevia

bullets.label: Painless vaginal bleeding, often sudden onset. Placenta partially or fully covers the cervical os.
⚠️ Vaginal examination is unsafe until placental location is confirmed by ultrasound.
Painful bleeding with uterine tenderness and rigidity. Premature separation of a normally sited placenta.
⚠️ Risk of haemorrhagic shock and fetal compromise — escalate urgently.

cards.title: Preterm Labour and Fetal Growth Concerns
cards.body: Prompt evaluation is essential when any of the following are present before term:

bullets.label: Rhythmic uterine tightening, especially with cervical change before 37 weeks
Prelabour rupture of membranes — assess colour, odour, and amount
Reduced fundal growth or small-for-dates findings require further investigation
Any perceived decrease in movement requires immediate assessment and CTG monitoring

cards.title: Clinical Scenario
cards.body: Recognising Severe Preeclampsia

bullets.label: A woman at 35 weeks presents with severe upper
bullets.text: A woman at 35 weeks presents with severe upper abdominal pain and visual disturbance. Her blood pressure is markedly elevated. The nurse recognises severe preeclampsia, initiates urgent escalation, prepares prescribed treatment, and monitors maternal and fetal status closely.

bullets.label: Recognise danger signs — do not wait for a doctor to identify urgency
Call for senior support using SBAR or local escalation protocol
Prepare antihypertensive and magnesium sulphate as prescribed
Continuous CTG monitoring and hourly urine output measurement
Identify danger signs and high BP.
Make an SBAR call to senior clinician.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Consolidate your understanding of high-risk maternal assessment with these essential principles:

bullets.label: Symptoms of severe preeclampsia are a medical emergency — act without delay
Never perform vaginal examination if placenta praevia has not been excluded
Maternal deterioration affects fetal wellbeing — assess both simultaneously
Use structured tools such as SBAR; accurate records support safe handover

cards.title: Ready to Continue Your GNPS Journey?
cards.body: Section 1 is complete. You have built a strong foundation in high-risk pregnancy recognition and maternal assessment — essential competencies for NCLEX preparation and international practice.

bullets.label: Revisit hypertensive disorders, diabetes, and placental complications
GNPS Programme 6 · Supporting Mothers and Newborns · Level 2 IQN · NCLEX Aligned

cards.title: Responding to Obstetric Emergencies
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 6 · Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse

cards.title: What Are Obstetric Emergencies?
cards.body: Obstetric emergencies develop suddenly and can threaten the life of the mother, fetus, or both. Rapid recognition and a coordinated response are critical to improving outcomes.

bullets.label: Every team member knows their task

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Identify key obstetric emergencies from clinical signs
Apply correct immediate responses for mother and fetus
Contribute effectively within a multi-disciplinary team
Provide accurate handover and emotional support under pressure

cards.title: Postpartum Haemorrhage (PPH)
cards.body: Rapid blood loss is one of the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide. Immediate action saves lives.

bullets.label: Call for emergency assistance without delay
Prepare and monitor transfusion as prescribed

cards.title: Cord Prolapse & Fetal Compromise
cards.body: Cord prolapse occurs when the umbilical cord descends ahead of the presenting part, compressing the cord and reducing fetal oxygenation. Every second counts.

bullets.label: Relieve pressure on the cord manually and immediately
Reposition the mother — knee-chest or Trendelenburg position
Call for emergency assistance and alert the obstetric team
Prepare for urgent birth — operative delivery is likely

cards.title: Shoulder Dystocia & Uterine Rupture
cards.body: Shoulder Dystocia

bullets.label: After delivery of the head, the anterior
bullets.text: After delivery of the head, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted. Apply established manoeuvres (HELPERR protocol): call for Help, Episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure, Enter, Remove arm, Roll.

bullets.label: A full-thickness tear of the uterine wall.
bullets.text: A full-thickness tear of the uterine wall. Signs include sudden severe pain, fetal bradycardia and maternal collapse. Requires immediate surgical intervention and resuscitation support.

bullets.label: Both emergencies demand immediate team
bullets.text: Both emergencies demand immediate team activation. Do not hesitate — call for senior obstetric support at the first sign.

cards.title: Amniotic Fluid Embolism & Collapse
cards.body: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is rare but rapidly fatal. Amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation, triggering cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia and coagulopathy.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Cord Prolapse in Action
cards.body: Following rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate falls sharply and the nurse observes the umbilical cord at the vaginal opening.

bullets.label: This scenario illustrates how rapid recognition
bullets.text: This scenario illustrates how rapid recognition and protocol-driven action can protect fetal oxygenation and facilitate a safe emergency birth.

cards.title: Effective Team Communication
cards.body: Clear, structured communication during obstetric emergencies prevents errors and ensures every team member is informed. Use closed-loop communication and structured handover tools.

bullets.label: Even in crisis, a calm tone and clear language
bullets.text: Even in crisis, a calm tone and clear language protect both the patient and team performance. Panic is contagious — composure saves lives.

bullets.label: Confirm verbal orders to avoid medication errors
Acknowledge the woman's fear; brief, reassuring statements

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Carry these principles into every clinical setting:

bullets.label: Do not manage obstetric emergencies alone. Call for support at the earliest sign of deterioration.
Follow evidence-based emergency protocols consistently. Preparation and practice improve response speed.
Maintain maternal and fetal oxygenation as the primary clinical priority throughout any emergency.
Structured, calm communication keeps the team aligned during rapidly evolving situations.
"Healthy beginnings. Compassionate care." — GNPS Programme 6 · Section 2 Complete

decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 6 - Level 2 - Section 3 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Caring for High-Risk Newborns
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Programme 6 · Section 3

cards.title: What Is a High-Risk Newborn?
cards.body: High-risk newborns require heightened vigilance. Their condition can deteriorate rapidly — making systematic assessment and timely intervention essential.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Assess a high-risk newborn using a structured, head-to-toe approach
Identify signs of respiratory distress, hypoglycaemia and neonatal sepsis
Support thermoregulation, feeding and oxygenation effectively
Communicate clearly with neonatal teams and families under pressure

cards.title: Prematurity and Low Birth Weight
cards.body: Premature newborns (born before 37 weeks) are particularly vulnerable. Their physiological immaturity affects multiple body systems simultaneously.

bullets.label: Thin skin and low fat stores impair thermoregulation
Immature lungs increase risk of respiratory difficulty
Weak suck reflex makes oral feeding challenging
Unstable blood sugar requires close monitoring
Developmentally supportive care — minimising
bullets.text: Developmentally supportive care — minimising stimulation and promoting skin-to-skin — is fundamental to premature newborn wellbeing.

cards.title: Recognising Respiratory Distress
cards.body: Why It Matters

bullets.label: Respiratory distress is one of the most urgent
bullets.text: Respiratory distress is one of the most urgent presentations in neonatal care. Each sign reflects increasing work of breathing and potential oxygen failure.

bullets.label: Apply prescribed oxygen or respiratory support
Escalate to neonatal team without delay

cards.title: Hypoglycaemia and Jaundice
cards.body: Hypoglycaemia

bullets.label: Blood glucose instability is common in
bullets.text: Blood glucose instability is common in premature, large-for-dates, and infants of diabetic mothers. Early feeding and glucose monitoring are critical.

bullets.label: Signs: jitteriness, poor tone, poor feeding, seizures
Management: early feeding, glucose gel or IV dextrose per policy
Visible yellowing of skin and sclera indicates
bullets.text: Visible yellowing of skin and sclera indicates rising bilirubin. Most is physiological but requires assessment and monitoring.

bullets.label: Appears day 2–3 in term infants; earlier is pathological
Treatment: phototherapy or exchange transfusion per severity
Assess risk factors and skin colour

cards.title: Neonatal Sepsis: Early Warning Signs
cards.body: Sepsis in newborns is life-threatening and can present subtly. A single unexplained change warrants prompt escalation.

bullets.label: Hypothermia or fever — either may indicate infection in the newborn
Reduced interest in feeding or weak suck is an early, often overlooked sign
Tachypnoea, apnoea or grunting may accompany systemic infection
Mottling, pallor, jaundice or lethargy all require immediate assessment
Early escalation and prompt antibiotic therapy
bullets.text: Early escalation and prompt antibiotic therapy are essential. Do not wait for culture results before initiating treatment if sepsis is suspected.

cards.title: Clinical Scenario: Applying Your Skills
cards.body: The Situation

bullets.label: A premature newborn develops grunting, chest retractions and falling oxygen saturation shortly after birth.
Maintains warmth — prevents cold stress worsening distress
Clear, timely communication with both the team and the family is as important as the clinical intervention itself.

cards.title: Nursing Priorities at a Glance
cards.body: Include Parents in Care

bullets.label: Involve families in decisions and updates whenever clinically possible — it supports bonding and reduces anxiety
Monitor blood glucose regularly in at-risk newborns; initiate feeding or therapy early
Use incubators, warm blankets or skin-to-skin care to prevent dangerous heat loss
Subtle changes matter — act on early signs of respiratory distress or sepsis immediately

cards.title: Section 3 Summary
cards.body: High-risk newborn care demands vigilance, rapid decision-making and compassionate communication. The principles from this section underpin safe neonatal practice across all clinical settings.

decks.title: Culturally Safe, Family-Centred Maternity Care
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 6 - Level 2 - Section 4 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Culturally Safe, Family-Centred Maternity Care
cards.body: "Healthy beginnings. Compassionate care."

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series
cards.body: What You Will Learn

bullets.label: By the end of this section, you will be
bullets.text: By the end of this section, you will be equipped to deliver respectful, informed and compassionate maternity care across diverse cultural contexts.

bullets.label: Provide care that respects individual values and practices
Support shared decision-making throughout the care journey
Use interpreters and accessible, adapted communication
Respond with compassion after loss, emergency or bereavement

cards.title: Why Cultural Safety Matters
cards.body: Maternity care does not happen in a vacuum — it unfolds within deeply personal, cultural and family contexts. International nurses must be mindful of this at every step.

bullets.label: Never presume preferences based on a woman's
bullets.text: Never presume preferences based on a woman's cultural background, ethnicity or religion. Always ask what matters most to her and her family.

bullets.label: Cultural practices — around birth, feeding,
bullets.text: Cultural practices — around birth, feeding, naming, or family roles — should be supported wherever it is clinically safe to do so.

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Informed Choice & Shared Decision-Making

bullets.label: Informed choice is not a single event — it is an ongoing process throughout pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period.
Present clear information on options, benefits, risks and alternatives
Allow sufficient time for questions and reflection
Confirm understanding without pressure or judgment
Revisit consent at each stage of care
Consent is never a one-time tick-box — it is a continuous, respectful conversation.

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Communication Access in Maternity Care

bullets.label: When to Use a Professional Interpreter
Family members — especially children — should not act as interpreters for clinical information.
Sign language interpreters or written communication
Plain language, visual aids and verbal explanation
Simplified steps, repetition and carer involvement

cards.title: Trauma, Loss & Bereavement
cards.body: Pregnancy loss, emergency birth and neonatal illness can be profoundly traumatic. Compassionate, trauma-informed care is essential — not optional.

bullets.label: Use calm, honest, sensitive language. Acknowledge grief without minimising it.
Ensure private spaces for families during difficult moments. Limit unnecessary interruptions.
Offer footprints, photographs or naming ceremonies where culturally and clinically appropriate.
Connect families with social workers, chaplaincy, counselling and peer support services.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Urgent Caesarean Birth: Respectful Care Under Pressure

bullets.label: A woman with limited English requires an urgent
bullets.text: A woman with limited English requires an urgent caesarean section. Even in high-pressure situations, respectful communication remains non-negotiable.

bullets.label: Key principle: Urgency does not remove the
bullets.text: Key principle: Urgency does not remove the right to respectful, informed communication. Adapt your approach — never abandon it.

cards.title: Applying the Framework
cards.body: Putting It All Together

bullets.label: Ask about preferences, language needs and cultural values at first contact
Arrange interpreters, adapt resources and involve family as directed by the woman
Provide care that is informed, respectful and trauma-sensitive throughout
Reflect on the interaction, document clearly and refer to additional support where needed

cards.title: NCLEX Preparation Focus
cards.body: Test Yourself

bullets.label: Common NCLEX-Style Themes in This Section
Questions on avoiding assumptions and accommodating diverse beliefs
Informed consent, autonomy and the right to refuse treatment
Use of professional interpreters and SBAR in urgent situations

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: 🙋 Ask, Don't Assume

bullets.label: Always ask what matters to the woman — never presume based on background
For complex, high-risk or sensitive discussions — every time
Support active involvement in decisions — even during urgent care
Provide trauma-informed, dignified care after any loss or emergency
GNPS Programme 6 · Section 4 Complete — Healthy beginnings. Compassionate care.
